prompt: On a memory-constrained embedded device, you must check whether any two readings in an array of 500,000 integers sum to a target. You are allowed to reorder the array. Which approach fits best? Here n is the number of readings.

options.text: Put every value in a hash set, checking for `target - x` as you go
options.explanation: With suitable hashing this gives expected linear work, but stores a set growing with the reading count. Its additional entries and table overhead do not fit the stated memory constraint.

options.text: Sort the array in place, then walk two pointers in from both ends
options.explanation: Correct. An in-place sort (such as heapsort) plus the two-pointer scan uses O(1) extra space, at the cost of O(n log n) time. Reordering is allowed, so mutating the input is fine. Here n is the input size or recursive argument stated in the question.

options.text: Copy the array, sort the copy, then use two pointers
options.explanation: This works but wastes O(n) memory on the copy, for no reason, since you are allowed to reorder the original. Here n is the input size or recursive argument stated in the question.

options.text: Check every pair with two nested loops
options.explanation: This uses constant extra space but quadratic time. The stated reading count implies roughly one hundred twenty-five billion pairs; sorting first retains the space saving with far less work.

workedExample: Memory is the binding constraint and reordering is allowed. Use a constant-auxiliary-space sort such as heapsort, then move two positions inward through the sorted array. A set or copied array adds storage proportional to reading count n. All-pairs search saves memory but does much more work. Assume fixed-width values and constant-cost arithmetic.

prompt: A service must hold ten million integers whose values fit a signed 64-bit representation. A measured Python-object representation exceeds its memory budget. Which alternative directly reduces per-item storage? Leave headroom for runtime and construction overhead.

options.text: A Python list of ints, since it is O(n) like any other option
options.explanation: A linear growth label does not remove the per-object and reference overhead that the scenario has measured.

options.text: A Python `set` of the ints, since sets are optimised for numbers
options.explanation: A set still stores objects and hash-table metadata; it does not pack the values into a fixed-width data buffer.

options.text: A packed array with verified eight-byte items
options.explanation: Correct. Fixed-width packed values avoid a separate Python integer object and reference slot per entry. Verify itemsize and supported value range.

options.text: No representation can improve memory because all are linear
options.explanation: Linear growth permits different per-item constants, which can decide whether a workload fits.

workedExample: Compare complete representations, not just growth labels. A packed eight-byte buffer uses 80 MB for ten million entries. A Python list additionally stores references and separate integer objects. Check array itemsize and value range on the target build, and leave headroom for runtime and temporary construction buffers.
